docs.title: plotviz
docs.text: plotviz is a desktop chart editor for scientists, engineers and analysts. Load tabular data, build publication-quality charts through a point-and-click interface, and export to PNG, SVG, PDF or JPEG — no code required.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• 26 chart types — Line, Scatter, Bar, Histogram, Boxplot, Violin, Pie, Polar, Radar, Heatmap, Contour, 3D Surface, and more
  • Curve fitting — 7 built-in models (Linear, Quadratic, Cubic, Exponential, Power Law, Logarithmic, Sigmoid) with confidence and prediction bands
  • Multi-panel layouts — 18 preset mosaic layouts plus a custom mosaic editor; each subplot is independently configured
  • Full style control — 10 built-in color schemes, 11 color palettes, per-curve style, grid, borders, fonts, and margins
  • Annotations — text labels, arrows, and image overlays with a drag-and-drop editor
  • Export — PNG, SVG, PDF, JPEG at any DPI and figure size

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Pre-built binaries (no Python required): Download macOS DMG / Windows ZIP → GitHub Releases

# from PyPI
pip install plotviz

Or run directly from source:

git clone https://github.com/pcachim/plotviz.git
cd plotviz
uv sync
uv run plotviz

See Getting Started for full setup instructions.

docs.title: Version
docs.text: Current release: 2.7.0 Requires Python 3.10+

docs.title: Axes
docs.text:
The Axes tab controls per-subplot axis configuration: the subplot title, axis labels, limits, scale, ticks, and the secondary Y axis. When the chart has more than one subplot, a Subplot selector at the top lets you switch between panels. Changing the selector in the Axes tab automatically syncs with the selectors in the other Plots pages.

From top to bottom (Equal scale is at the very top):

  1. X axis — Label (text, font, size, colour, rotation, position), limits or auto limits, the scale (linear, log, logit, inverted), tick size, direction, minor ticks, step, format, and where the axis sits.
  2. Y axis (left) — The same settings for the left y axis.
  3. Y axis (right / secondary) — The same for the secondary axis, active when a series has Y2 ticked.

docs.title: Subplot title
docs.text:
The Subplot Title section is at the top of the tab and only appears when the chart has more than one panel. For a single-panel chart, the chart title is set in the Layout & Style tab.

Control Description Show title Checkbox: toggle title visibility Text field Title text for this subplot Font / Size / Color Typography Pad Distance between the title and the top of the axes (points) Rot Rotation in degrees Align center, left or right

docs.title: Axis labels
docs.text:
Each axis (X, Y, Y2) has three controls:

Control Description Show label Checkbox — hide the label without clearing the text Text field The label text (placeholder shows the column name when empty) Font / Size / Color Typography for the label

When the text is empty the axis is titled with the names of the data series; fitted curves are left out of that default, so adding several fits does not lengthen the title (type a label if you want the fits named).

X and Y label fonts and colors are global — they apply to all subplots. Per-subplot overrides are not available for axis labels.

docs.title: Axis limits
docs.text:
Control Description Auto Checkbox — let matplotlib choose limits automatically (default on) Min / Max Manual limit values, active only when Auto is off

Uncheck Auto and set Min/Max to zoom into a specific data range without changing the data itself.

docs.title: Axis scale
docs.text:
Four radio buttons set the scale for each axis:

Scale Description Linear Uniform spacing (default) Log Logarithmic spacing — requires all data > 0 Logit Logit scale for probabilities (0–1) Inverted Linear scale with the axis reversed (high values at the left/bottom)

docs.title: Tick marks
docs.text: Control Description Show ticks Checkbox — hide tick marks and labels entirely Tick size Font size for tick labels (pt) Tick direction out (default), in, or inout Minor ticks Checkbox — show minor tick marks between major ticks Rotation Angle of tick labels in degrees (useful for long X labels) Step Force a fixed interval between major ticks (0 = automatic)

docs.title: Tick formatters
docs.text:
The Formatter dropdown on each axis controls how tick values are displayed:

Formatter Example output auto matplotlib default plain 1234567 (no scientific notation) sci 1.23 × 10⁶ percent 12.3% {x:.2f}, {x:.0f}, … any Python format string with {x}: 3.14, 3 %Y-%m-%d, %d/%m/%Y, %b %Y, %H:%M, … a date format, for an axis that shows dates

The dropdown is editable, so you can type any format. Date formats only make sense on an axis that shows a date column; see Date and time columns. With auto, a date axis picks sensible ticks and labels by itself (years, months, days or hours, depending on the range).

docs.title: Secondary Y axis (Y2)
docs.text:
Enable the secondary Y axis by ticking the Y2 checkbox on one or more series rows in Plots → Plot. The Y2 axis appears on the right side of the plot.

In the Axes tab, the Y2 section provides the same controls as the primary Y axis: label text/font/size/color, limits (auto or manual).

docs.title: Subplot spacing
docs.text:
When the chart has more than one subplot, two sliders in the Axes tab control the spacing between panels:

Control Description H space Vertical gap between rows of subplots (height fraction) W space Horizontal gap between columns of subplots (width fraction)

docs.title: Canvas & Grid
docs.text:
The Plots → Canvas & Grid page sets the look of the plot area of one subplot: its colour, which borders are drawn, and the grid. With several subplots, the Editing selector at the top of the Plots tab chooses which one. The figure background and the colours of text and axes belong to the whole figure and are in Color Schemes.

From top to bottom:

  1. Chart canvas — The colour of the plot area and which borders (top, bottom, left, right) are drawn.
  2. Grid — The major and minor grid: switch each on, and set colour, line style, width and opacity (α).

docs.title: Plot area
docs.text: The colour of the plot area, the inner background inside the axes. With several subplots each one has its own: changing it here is a local adjustment of this subplot and does not change the colour scheme.

docs.title: Borders (spines)
docs.text: Four checkboxes — Top, Bottom, Left, Right — show or hide the four axis border lines (spines). Hiding the top and right spines is a common convention for scientific plots.

docs.title: Grid
docs.text:
Control Description Show grid Toggle the major grid on/off Grid color Color of major grid lines Line style Solid, dashed, dotted, or dash-dot Line width Stroke thickness (0.1–5.0) Alpha Grid line opacity (0.0–1.0) Show minor grid Toggle the minor grid (sub-divisions between major ticks)

Minor grid controls (color, style, width, alpha) mirror the major grid controls.

docs.title: Chart Types
docs.text: plotviz supports 26 chart types. Types marked per-series can be mixed freely in the same subplot. Types marked whole-chart take over the entire panel and cannot be combined with other types.

docs.title: Per-series types
docs.text: These types are assigned per row in the series table. Multiple series with different types can share the same subplot axes.

docs.title: Line
docs.text:
A classic line chart connecting data points in X order. Default options:

  • Line style — solid, dashed, dotted, dash-dot, or none.
  • Line width — stroke thickness in points.
  • Marker — point shape (circle, square, triangle, cross, diamond, etc.) or none.
  • Marker size — size of each point marker.
  • Color — line and marker fill color.

Configured in the Series tab.

docs.title: Scatter
docs.text: Plots each (X, Y) pair as an independent point with no connecting line. Options: point size, alpha (opacity), color.

docs.title: Bar
docs.text:
Vertical grouped bars. One bar per data point, one group per X value. Options:

  • Width — bar width as a fraction of available space (0.05–1.0, default 0.8).
  • Stacked — accumulates bars vertically instead of grouping side by side.
  • Horizontal — rotates the chart 90° (bars grow left/right).

docs.title: Errorbar
docs.text: Line chart with error bars drawn at each point. Requires a column assigned to the Error dropdown below the series table. Options: Cap size (length of the horizontal cap lines).

docs.title: Area
docs.text:
Filled region between the line and the X axis (or between two lines if stacked). Options:

  • Fill alpha — transparency of the filled region (0.05–1.0, default 0.4).
  • Stacked — accumulates areas vertically.

docs.title: Fill Between
docs.text:
The area between a series and a second series (the Fill Between Y2 dropdown), or between the series and the X axis when none is chosen. Options:

  • Alpha — transparency of the filled region.
  • Line width and Show line — the outlines of the two curves.

docs.title: Step
docs.text: Like Line but uses a staircase interpolation between points instead of straight lines. Useful for discrete or sampled data, histograms drawn as steps.

docs.title: Stem
docs.text: Draws vertical lines (stems) from the X axis to each data point, with a marker at the tip. Good for sparse discrete signals.

docs.title: Bubble
docs.text:
Scatter chart where the size of each point is controlled by a third column assigned to the Z dropdown. Options:

  • Size col — which column drives the bubble radius (or "(uniform)" for equal sizes).
  • Scale — multiplier applied to Z values to compute pixel radius.
  • Alpha — fill opacity.
  • Marker — point shape.
  • Edge color — outline color around each bubble.

docs.title: Waterfall
docs.text:
Cumulative bar chart where each bar starts where the previous one ended. Positive increments grow upward (green by default), negative increments fall (red). Options:

  • Show connectors — horizontal lines linking the top/bottom of adjacent bars.
  • Bar width — width as a fraction of cell.
  • Pos color / Neg color — colors for positive and negative bars.
  • Alpha — fill opacity.

docs.title: Whole-chart types
docs.text: These types use all series columns together and cannot be mixed with other types in the same subplot.

docs.title: Histogram
docs.text:
Distribution of a single Y column. Options:

  • Bins — number of histogram bins (2–500, default 20).
  • Density — normalize the Y axis to show probability density instead of counts.

docs.title: Hist2D
docs.text: 2D histogram (heatmap of point density) using X and Y columns together. Options: Colormap, Bins.

docs.title: Hexbin
docs.text: Like Hist2D but aggregates points into hexagonal cells. Options: Colormap, Bins.

docs.title: Boxplot
docs.text: Box-and-whisker plots showing median, quartiles and outliers for one or more Y columns. Multiple series produce side-by-side boxes.

docs.title: Violin
docs.text:
Kernel-density estimate of the distribution, mirrored to form a violin shape. Options:

  • Show means — horizontal line at the mean.
  • Show medians — horizontal line at the median.
  • Show extrema — lines at the minimum and maximum.
  • Points — number of points in the KDE (100/200/500/1000).
  • bw_method — bandwidth selection for the KDE (scott or silverman).
  • Vertical — draw violins vertically (default) or horizontally.

docs.title: Pie
docs.text:
Circular sector chart. Each Y value becomes a slice whose angle is proportional to its share of the total. Options:

  • Show % — print the percentage inside each slice.
  • Shadow — drop shadow under the pie.

docs.title: Polar
docs.text:
Line or scatter chart in polar coordinates. X is the angle (radians), Y is the radius. Options:

  • Line style, Line width, Marker — visual style.
  • Fill — fill the area under the polar line.

docs.title: Radar
docs.text: Spider/radar chart. Each column in the Y data becomes one axis radiating from the center. Multiple series are overlaid. Useful for comparing multivariate profiles.

docs.title: Heatmap
docs.text:
2D color grid. Requires a Z column. Plots X values along one axis, Y values along the other, and colors cells by Z. Options:

  • Colormap — matplotlib colormap (viridis, plasma, coolwarm, etc.).
  • Show colorbar — display the color scale legend.

docs.title: Contour
docs.text:
Contour or filled contour plot of a 2D scalar field. Requires X, Y and Z columns on a regular or irregular grid. Options:

  • Colormap — color mapping for the contour levels.
  • Contour levels — number of isolines (3–100, default 10).

docs.title: Tricontour
docs.text:
Contour plot of a scalar field known at scattered points (no regular grid needed): the points are triangulated. Requires X, Y and Z columns. Options:

  • Fill — Filled contour, Face colours (one colour per triangle) or None.
  • Levels, Alpha and Colormap.
  • Lines — contour lines over the fill; Triangulation shows the triangles.
  • Colorbar and its size.

docs.title: 3D Surface
docs.text: Three-dimensional surface plot. Requires X, Y and Z columns. The canvas renders in 3D; rotate the view by clicking and dragging.

docs.title: ECDF
docs.text: Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function. Plots the fraction of data points ≤ each X value. Useful for comparing distributions without binning.

docs.title: Quiver
docs.text:
Vector field plot: an arrow at each (X, Y) point. The direction and length of the arrow come from two columns chosen in the U (horizontal component) and V (vertical component) dropdowns. Options:

  • Scale — arrow length scale (1.0 = automatic).
  • Width — shaft width.
  • Color by magnitude — colour each arrow by its length, with a Colormap.

docs.title: Barbs
docs.text:
Meteorological wind barbs: at each (X, Y) point a staff with flags and feathers whose number tells the wind speed, pointing along the U and V components. Options:

  • Length — length of the staff in points.
  • Pivot — which end of the staff sits on the point (tip or middle).
  • Alpha — opacity.
  • Color by magnitude — colour by speed, with a Colormap.

docs.title: Streamplot
docs.text:
Streamlines of a vector field. X and Y must be the points of a regular grid (every x with every y, for example from Generate → (u,v)=f(x,y) with Meshgrid), with the field components in the U and V dropdowns. Options:

  • Density — how closely the lines are packed.
  • Arrow size and Line width.
  • Color by magnitude — colour by speed, with a Colormap.

docs.title: Chart-type options panel
docs.text: When a whole-chart type is active, a corresponding options panel appears in the Data tab below the series table. Per-series options (line style, marker, color) are set in the Series tab regardless of chart type.

docs.title: Python Code Runner
docs.text:
The Python Code Runner is a built-in code editor that lets you write arbitrary Python code — using matplotlib, seaborn, numpy, pandas, or any installed library — and render the resulting chart in a live preview pane, all without leaving plotviz.

Open it from the menu bar: Tools → Python Code Runner…

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
The window is split into two panels:

Panel Contents Left — editor Syntax-highlighted Python editor with toolbar, status bar, run button, and error panel Right — preview Live matplotlib canvas with navigation toolbar and export controls

docs.title: Editor toolbar
docs.text: Button Action 📂 Open… Load code from a .py file 📦 Load .pvizx… Load and immediately run a Python Export bundle (.pvizx) 💾 Save… Save the current editor contents to a .py file ✕ Clear Clear the editor ↺ Sample Restore the built-in sample chart code

docs.title: Writing code
docs.text: The editor supports full Python syntax with highlighting for keywords, strings, comments, numbers, and function names.

docs.title: Available shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl + Enter (or Cmd + Enter on macOS) Run the code Tab Indent the selected block Shift + Tab Dedent the selected block

docs.title: Namespace
docs.text:
When your code runs, the following names are available without any import:

Name Type Contents np / numpy module NumPy plt / matplotlib module Matplotlib and pyplot mpl module matplotlib root module pd / pandas module Pandas (if installed) sns / seaborn module Seaborn (if installed) scipy module SciPy (if installed) datasets dict All columns currently loaded in plotviz — keys are column names, values are NumPy arrays

You can import any other installed package normally inside your code.

docs.title: Using plotviz datasets
docs.text:
If you have data loaded in the plotviz Data tab, you can reference those columns directly:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = datasets['time']       # NumPy array
y = datasets['pressure']

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y, linewidth=1.8)
ax.set_xlabel('Time (s)')
ax.set_ylabel('Pressure (Pa)')
plt.tight_layout()

docs.title: Figure requirements
docs.text:
Your code must create at least one matplotlib figure (plt.figure(), plt.subplots(), or a seaborn figure-level function). If it runs without producing a figure, a message is shown in the preview canvas.

If your code creates multiple figures, the last one is displayed in the preview.

docs.title: Running code
docs.text:
Click ▶ Run Code or press Ctrl + Enter. The canvas updates immediately.

All matplotlib figures from a previous run are closed before each new run, so stale figures never accumulate.

docs.title: Error panel
docs.text:
If your code raises an exception, a collapsible error panel appears below the editor showing the full Python traceback. The canvas shows a brief error notice on the right.

Button Action Copy Copy the full traceback to the clipboard ✕ Dismiss the error panel

Fix the code and run again — the error panel hides automatically at the start of each successful run.

docs.title: Loading a .pvizx bundle
docs.text:
A .pvizx file is a Python Export bundle generated by File → Export Python Bundle (.pvizx)…. It contains a standalone plot.py script and the chart's data as CSV files.

Click 📦 Load .pvizx… to open a bundle. plotviz extracts the archive, loads plot.py into the editor, and runs it automatically. You can then inspect, edit, or extend the generated code.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
After running, you can save the rendered chart using the Export… button in the bottom-right corner.

Control Description DPI spinner Export resolution (72–600 DPI, default 150) Export… Save as PNG, SVG, PDF, or JPEG

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: The Code Runner window hides rather than closes when you press Escape or the close button — your code is preserved for the session. Re-opening it from the menu restores the editor exactly as you left it.

docs.title: Color Schemes
docs.text: A color scheme is a named preset that applies a coordinated set of colors to the chart background, plot area, foreground, grid, and text all at once. Color schemes do not affect individual series colors or axis limits.

docs.title: Built-in color schemes
docs.text: Name Character Palette Default (white) Clean white background Matplotlib Ivory Ivory, no grid, only left/bottom spines Publication Blueprint (light) Ice-blue, solid major and minor grid Cool Grey panel Grey plot area, thick white grid, no spines Matplotlib Graph paper Pale green, dense fine grid Earth Newsprint Cream-salmon, bottom spine only Colorblind Solarized (light) Solarized beige, dashed grid Warm Lavender Lilac, white plot area, dotted grid Ocean Sage Grey-green, white plot area Nature Dark (charcoal) Deep charcoal #1e1e2e, light text Bold Dark (slate) Navy #0f172a, slate plot area Bold Midnight blue Deep blue, cyan axis labels Bold High contrast Black background, white text Bold

docs.title: Applying a color scheme
docs.text:
1. Open the Layout & Style tab.
  2. Choose a scheme from the Color Schemes dropdown. It is applied at once; use Ctrl+Z to undo.
  3. With several subplots, Apply to chooses All subplots (the default) or Active subplot only. The second changes just that subplot's plot area, axes colour, borders, grid and title colour; the figure background, palette, fonts and axis-label colours belong to the whole figure and stay as they are. Pick the active subplot with the Editing selector in the Plots tab.

The five colored swatches next to the dropdown show a preview of BG, Plot, FG, Grid, and Title colors for the selected scheme.

docs.title: The active scheme
docs.text:
The scheme shown in the dropdown is the active scheme: the colours of the chart are that scheme. It tracks the eight colours (figure and plot background, foreground, title, X and Y labels, grid and minor grid), whether the grid, minor grid and each border are shown, and the palette. Fonts, sizes and grid line style are applied with a scheme but are not tracked.

  • Built-in schemes are read-only. The first time you change anything they track, plotviz makes an editable copy, <name> – edited, and makes it active. Every further change goes into that copy. If you change everything back, the copy is dropped.
  • Your own schemes (made with Edit scheme… or loaded from a file) are edited in place.
  • Switching schemes never loses anything during the session: the scheme you leave stays in the dropdown.
  • A * after a name means the scheme is not in the schemes folder, so it will not be there next time. Saving it into the folder removes the *.
  • With several subplots, the grid, plot background, foreground and borders are per subplot. Changing them there is a local adjustment and does not touch the scheme, and Apply to: Active subplot only leaves the active scheme as it is.
  • A chart file (.pviz) stores its active scheme, name and values, so the chart looks the same when reopened.

docs.title: Editing a color scheme
docs.text: Click Edit in the Color Schemes section to create or change a scheme in one place: the eight colours, grid and border switches and the palette. Load from starts from another scheme. Save & apply names the scheme, makes it active and applies it. Built-in names cannot be replaced.

docs.title: Background and foreground colours
docs.text:
The figure background and the foreground are edited in the scheme editor (Edit in the Color Schemes section). The plot area can also be changed on the Canvas & Grid page.

  • Chart BG — the outer figure background (outside the plot area). Default white.
  • Plot BG — the inner plot area background. Default white.
  • Foreground — the default color for axes, tick marks, tick labels, and spines. Default black.

Click any color swatch to open the color picker. The picker includes a Recent colors row (up to 8 previously selected colors) above the Custom colors section, so frequently used colors are always one click away.

docs.title: Saving a color scheme
docs.text: Click Save in the Color Schemes section. The dialog opens in the schemes folder (~/Library/Application Support/plotviz/schemes/ on macOS; Preferences shows it and can open it), and every .pvizc there is loaded when plotviz starts. You may save elsewhere, but then the scheme keeps its * and is not loaded at start-up. Built-in schemes cannot be saved. To delete a scheme, delete its file.

docs.title: Loading a color scheme
docs.text: Click Load and select a single .pvizc file, for instance one from outside the folder. You are asked whether to apply it, and applying it makes it the active scheme. A .pvizt template file can also be loaded as a color source — only the color-related settings are extracted.

docs.title: Curves and Fitting
docs.text:
The Curves page of the Plots tab controls the visual appearance of individual curves and provides curve fitting tools.

When the chart has more than one subplot, a Subplot selector at the top switches context. The curve selector below it lists all series assigned to the active subplot.

docs.title: Per-curve style
docs.text:
The Plots → Curves page:

  1. Per-curve — Choose the curve, then its line style, colour (Unlock lets the palette change it again), marker, line width and marker size, marker colour and draw style.
  2. Curve fit (line / scatter) — The model and the options of the fit (range of x, weights, robust), Apply Fit and Remove Fit, the list of fits of the chart with their R², RMSE and AIC, the confidence and prediction bands, and the results.

Select a series from the Curve dropdown to edit its style. Changes take effect on the live preview immediately.

docs.title: Line
docs.text: Control Description Line style Solid (-), dashed (--), dotted (:) , dash-dot (-.), or none Line width Stroke thickness in points Color Line color — click the swatch to open the color picker Lock color When checked, auto-palette assignment does not override the manually chosen color

docs.title: Marker
docs.text: Control Description Marker Point shape: circle, square, triangle up/down/left/right, diamond, pentagon, hexagon, star, plus, cross, x, or None Marker size Point size in points Marker color Independent color for the marker fill (defaults to the line color)

docs.title: Color auto-assignment
docs.text: When a palette is active (set in the Layout & Style tab), plotviz assigns the next palette color to each new series automatically. If Lock color is off, switching palettes reassigns all unlocked series colors to match the new palette. Lock a color to keep it fixed across palette changes.

docs.title: Curve fitting
docs.text: The curve fitting section lets you fit a mathematical model to any series and overlay the result on the chart.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Select the series to fit in the Per-Curve selector above. (If a fit curve is selected, the series it came from is fitted.)
  2. Choose a model from the Model dropdown.
  3. Click Apply Fit.
  4. The fitted curve appears on the chart and the equation and statistics are shown in the results box.

docs.title: Available models
docs.text:
Model Equation Typical use Linear y = a·x + b Quadratic y = a·x² + b·x + c Cubic y = a·x³ + b·x² + c·x + d Polynomial (degree n) y = cn·xⁿ + … + c1·x + c0 any degree from 1 to 10; choose the Degree below the list Exponential y = a·e^(b·x) decay or growth towards 0 Exponential + offset y = a·e^(b·x) + c charging or discharging (a capacitor, cooling): it settles at c instead of 0 Power Law y = a·x^b needs x > 0 Logarithmic y = a·ln(x) + b needs x > 0 Sigmoid y = a / (1 + e^(−(x − b)/c)) rising or falling step Gaussian y = a·e^(−(x − μ)²/2σ²) + c a peak (or, with a < 0, a dip) on a baseline: centre μ, width σ, height a Sinusoid y = a·sin(2π·f·x + φ) + c a periodic signal: amplitude, frequency (cycles per x unit), phase Custom expression whatever you type see below Smoothing (LOWESS) no equation a smooth trend through noisy data, to see its shape; see below

Fitted parameters are shown in the results box along with R², RMSE, and other statistics.

docs.title: Custom expression
docs.text:
Type the formula in Custom expression, for example a*exp(-x/b) + c or a*x/(b+x):

  • x is the independent variable; every other letter or word is a parameter to fit. The results list them in the order they first appear.
  • You can use numbers, + - * / ** %, parentheses, the constants pi and e, and the functions sin cos tan arcsin arccos arctan arctan2 sinh cosh tanh exp expm1 log log10 log2 log1p sqrt cbrt abs sign minimum maximum. Nothing else is accepted (no attributes, no other function calls, no conditions).
  • Start values (optional): a=3, b=2, c=1. The search starts at 1 for the parameters you do not list (and also tries 0.1 and 10). Give them when the fit does not converge.
  • The F-test is not defined for custom models; use the AIC to compare.

Polynomials, the Gaussian, the sinusoid and the offset exponential find their own starting values from the data (the sinusoid from the spectrum, so a frequency is found without being given). A negative width or amplitude is reported in its usual form: σ > 0, a > 0 with the phase turned half a cycle.

docs.title: What to fit
docs.text:
Below the model, three options decide which points count and how much:

  • Fit only x from … to …: only the points in that stretch decide the fit, to leave out a transient or a zone without interest. Leave a box empty for no limit; write a date when x is a date. The curve is still drawn over all of x, and the results say how many points were left out.
  • Weight by the error column: points with a larger error count less. It uses the Error column chosen in the Plot tab (so it is available only when one is chosen), read as the standard deviation of each y. The results show χ² and the reduced χ² (near 1 when the errors match the scatter), the parameter errors are absolute, and there is no F test. Points whose error is missing or not positive are left out.
  • Robust (reduce the effect of outliers): points far from the curve count less, so a few wild values do not drag the fit, and the ones that stand out (more than 3 robust standard deviations from it) are counted as outliers in the results. R² and RMSE still include them, and the parameter errors are approximate.

Each combination is a fit of its own: its name carries what was chosen (Series 1 (Linear, x 2–…, robust fit)), so you can fit a series with and without an option and compare them in the Fits list. The prediction band uses the scatter of the points that were fitted.

docs.title: Smoothing (LOWESS)
docs.text: LOWESS draws a smooth trend through the data by fitting a short line around each point, using the share of points set by Span (0.05 to 1; small follows the data closely, large is smoother). It is for seeing a trend without choosing a model: it has no equation, parameters, bands or tests, and it is not drawn outside the range of the data. It is saved with the chart and shows in the Fits list with its R² and RMSE.

docs.title: How the data are handled
docs.text:
• Missing values. Points where x or y is NaN are ignored, and the results say how many.
  • Starting values for the Exponential, Power Law and Sigmoid models come from the data (for example the Exponential starts from a straight-line fit of ln y), so they work for any amplitude and x range, for decreasing sigmoids, and for negative data.
  • x far from zero (years, or a date column, which is a number of days since 1970): the fit is done on x − x₀, where x₀ is about the centre of the data, because e^(b·19800) overflows and polynomials in such x are badly conditioned. The equation then shows (x − x₀) and the results box gives x₀. The curve and the bands are still drawn against the real x.
  • Logarithmic and Power Law need every x to be greater than 0; if not, the fit reports it instead of returning a meaningless curve.
  • A fit that does not converge is reported with a message, never drawn as a curve with a nonsense R².
  • The fit curve and its bands are drawn from left to right even when the data are not sorted by x.

docs.title: Several fits of the same series
docs.text:
You can apply as many models as you like to a series, to compare them. Every fit is kept, with its own parameters, statistics, bands and style, and all of them are saved in the .pviz file.

The Fits list under the buttons shows them side by side:

Column Meaning Show Untick to hide the fit and its bands from the chart (and from the exported script) without deleting it Model, Series What was fitted to what R², RMSE, AIC The numbers to compare by. The bold AIC is the lowest among the fits of that series: a better fit relative to its number of parameters. A higher-order model always has a higher R², so look at the AIC before choosing it

Click a row to select that fit: the confidence limits, the prediction band, the style controls and the results below then act on it. Selecting a fit curve in the Per-Curve list does the same.

  • Each new fit takes a colour that the series and its other fits do not use, so they can be told apart.
  • Applying the same model to the same series again replaces the previous one, and the results say so.
  • Remove Fit removes the selected fit only. With the data series selected it removes all its fits, after asking.
  • The results box shows the selected fit; it never shows another one instead.

docs.title: Fit curve style
docs.text:
The appearance of the fitted curve is set independently from the data series:

Control Description Color Color of the fit line Line style Solid, dashed, dotted, etc. Line width Stroke thickness

docs.title: Confidence and prediction bands
docs.text:
Control Description Confidence limits Shaded region around the fit: Off, 1σ (68%), 2σ (95%) or 3σ (99.7%) Prediction band Shaded region where new observations are expected to fall: Off, 1σ, 2σ or 3σ Band opacity Opacity of the shaded bands (0.05–1.0; 0.35 by default, the prediction band is drawn at half of it)

The bands belong to the fit curve and are drawn whatever line type you give that curve, and they follow it if you rename it. If the data lie exactly on the curve (for example data made by the function generator, with no noise) the bands have no width and cannot be seen; the results box says so.

When a fit curve is selected and you click Apply Fit with another model, the new model is fitted to the data the curve came from, not to the curve (a curve fitted to its own fit would fit perfectly and have bands of no width).

The percentages hold for few points too: the bands use the Student-t quantile for the degrees of freedom of the fit, which for many points is the same as 1, 2 or 3 normal standard deviations.

The confidence band is tighter (it bounds the mean prediction); the prediction band is wider (it bounds individual future observations).

docs.title: Fit results
docs.text:
The results box at the bottom of the section shows:

  • Model equation with fitted parameter values
  • Goodness of fit: n, parameters, degrees of freedom, R², adjusted R², RMSE, MSE, SSE, SST, AIC and BIC (from the Gaussian log-likelihood, as in statsmodels)
  • F-statistic and its p-value, for the models that contain an intercept-only model (Linear, Quadratic, Cubic, Logarithmic); the Exponential, Power Law and Sigmoid have no such test and show —
  • For each parameter: value, standard error, t, p and the confidence interval

The fit result is saved with the .pviz project file and restored on reload.

docs.title: Datasets and Import
docs.text:
The Data → Datasets page loads your files and lists every column the chart can use.

The Datasets page of the Data tab:

  1. Datasets — Browse Files opens the import dialog. The list below shows every column loaded, from files and also those created by Generate, Transform and curve fits; select one or more to act on them. Remove selected deletes the selected columns, Inspect values shows a summary and lets you edit them.

Open the Data tab and click Browse Files to load one or more data files. Supported formats:

Format Extensions Notes CSV .csv Separator, decimal mark and encoding selectable Excel .xlsx, .xls Choose the sheet in the import dialog JSON .json Array of objects or column-oriented dict Plain text .txt Whitespace-separated columns

Each file opens an import dialog with a preview of the first 100 rows. You can pick the columns to import and rename them. Numeric columns become float arrays, date columns become dates (below), and other text columns are treated as categorical. Column names are taken from the first row.

docs.title: Import options
docs.text:
Option Applies to Purpose Sheet Excel Which sheet to read Separator CSV, TXT Auto-detect, comma, semicolon, tab, whitespace, pipe or a custom character Decimal CSV, TXT Point (1.5) or Comma (1,5). Use the comma for files from European locales, otherwise numbers such as 1,5 are read as text Encoding CSV, TXT utf-8-sig (the default) reads plain UTF-8 and the marker Excel adds at the start of the file; try latin-1 or cp1252 if accented characters look wrong Orientation JSON Layout of the JSON data Header row, Skip rows All Where the column names are, and how many lines to ignore before them

You can load multiple files in one session — each file's columns are pooled into the shared column list and available in all series rows.

docs.title: Date and time columns
docs.text:
Columns that hold dates or times are recognised when you import them and marked with 📅 in the column list. They can be used as the X (or Y) of any series, and the axis then shows dates, with ticks that adapt to the range: years, months, days, hours…

Recognised formats include 2024-03-01, 2024-03-01 12:30, 2024-03-01T12:30:00, 1 Mar 2024, March 5, 2024 and 03/04/2024, and Excel date cells. A text column is only taken as dates when every value looks like a date, so names such as May or numbers such as 1,5 stay as they were. Two import options control this:

Option Purpose Dates: auto-detect / off Turn the detection off to keep date-like columns as plain text Day first Read 03/04/2024 as 3 April instead of March 4

Things to know:

  • A date column is kept as the number of days since 1970-01-01 (fractions are the time of day), so everything that works on numbers keeps working: transforms, fits, statistics. Time zones are converted to UTC and dropped.
  • The tick labels follow the range automatically. To choose them, type a date format such as %d/%m/%Y in the axis Format box (Axes).
  • Limits and the tick step typed in the Axes tab are in days (for example a step of 7 puts a tick every week).
  • Log scales are ignored on a date axis.
  • Saved charts keep dates as dates, and so does the Python export.
  • The Seaborn Explorer and the Code Runner see date columns as numbers (days since 1970-01-01). In the Code Runner use pd.to_datetime(x, unit='D') to get datetimes back.

docs.title: Removing datasets
docs.text: Select one or more entries in the Datasets list and click Remove selected. Any series that reference removed columns will show empty dropdowns but are not deleted from the table.

docs.title: Inspecting columns
docs.text:
Select a column (or multiple columns) in the Datasets list and click Inspect values to see a summary: count, min, max, mean, and a preview of the first values.

For a full summary (quartiles, standard deviation, skewness, correlation between series), use the Statistics page; to create new series from existing ones (smoothing, derivatives, resampling…), use the Transform page. See Statistics and Transform.

docs.title: File Formats
docs.text: plotviz uses four proprietary file formats, all of which are ZIP archives containing JSON metadata. They can be inspected or manipulated with any ZIP tool.

docs.title: .pviz — Chart project
docs.text:
A .pviz file is a complete saved chart. It contains:

Entry Contents settings.json All style, axis, and layout settings series.json Series table rows, subplot assignments, Z and error column selections data.json Dataset columns (all columns or used-only, depending on save choice). Date columns are stored as ISO 8601 text palette.json The active palette's definition, when it is one of your own images/ Embedded image files referenced by image annotations

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: Choose File → Save Chart (Ctrl+S). It rewrites the open file without asking; the first time, or with Save Chart As… (Ctrl+Shift+S), a dialog asks where to save. A dialog asks whether to save Used series only (keeps only the columns currently assigned in the series table) or All columns (preserves every loaded column for future reassignment). Used-only files are smaller; all-columns files are more portable. All columns is the default button (Enter) and sits on the right, with Cancel on the left. If every loaded column is already used, nothing is asked.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text: Choose File → Open Chart… (Ctrl+O), or double-click a .pviz file in Finder/Explorer. The chart, all datasets, and all settings are restored exactly.

docs.title: Recent files
docs.text: The last 12 opened .pviz files appear in File → Open Recent for quick access.

docs.title: .pvizt — Template
docs.text:
A .pvizt file saves all style and layout settings but contains no data. Use templates to apply a consistent visual style across multiple charts.

Entry Contents settings.json Style, axis, layout, and annotation defaults (_file_type: "template")

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: Select Save Template (.pvizt) from the save dropdown.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text: Select Load Template (.pvizt) from the open dropdown, or double-click a .pvizt file. The template's settings are applied to the current chart; existing data and series assignments are preserved.

docs.title: .pvizc — Color scheme
docs.text:
A .pvizc file is a minimal settings file containing only color-related keys: background, foreground, plot area, grid, title/label colors, border visibility, and the palette name. It also carries the palette's 16 colours (_palette), so the scheme looks the same on a machine that lacks that palette. It does not contain axis limits, figure size, data, or series assignments.

Entry Contents settings.json Color keys only (_file_type: "color_scheme", _scheme_name)

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, Color Schemes section, click Save (or File → Save Scheme…). The dialog opens in the schemes folder, whose .pvizc files are loaded when plotviz starts; the file name is the scheme name.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
Click Load to open a single .pvizc file. The scheme is registered in the Color Schemes dropdown (marked * when the file is outside the schemes folder) and you are asked whether to apply it immediately.

Double-clicking a .pvizc file in Finder/Explorer applies it to the current chart silently.

docs.title: .pvizp — Palette bundle
docs.text:
A .pvizp file holds one of your color palettes so it can be kept, shared or used on another machine. Every .pvizp in the palettes folder is loaded when plotviz starts.

Entry Contents palette.json The palette definition (name → list of 16 hex colors)

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, click Save under Colour palette (or File → Save Palette…). The active palette is saved; built-in palettes are not.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
Click Load under Colour palette. The palette is added to the current session (you are asked whether to apply it) and is marked as saved.

Double-clicking a .pvizp file in Finder/Explorer imports it.

docs.title: Internal structure
docs.text:
All four formats are standard ZIP archives. To inspect a file:

# macOS / Linux
unzip -p myfile.pviz settings.json | python3 -m json.tool

# Windows PowerShell
Expand-Archive myfile.pviz -DestinationPath .\extracted\

The _app, _version, and _file_type keys in settings.json identify the format. plotviz reads files with any version and applies safe defaults for keys that are missing, so older files remain compatible with newer releases.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text: The Data → Generate page creates series without loading a file: the y=f(x), z=f(x,y) and (u,v)=f(x,y) generators, and the Table for typing values. To derive new series from loaded ones, see Transform.

docs.title: Function Generator
docs.text:
The function generator evaluates a mathematical expression over a range of X values and adds the result as a new dataset.

The Generate page, y=f(x):

  1. Function generator — The input is either an x range (from, to, number of points, spacing and the name of the x column) or an existing column; then the expression and the name of the y column. Generate / Apply at the bottom creates the columns.
  2. Preview — What the button would create. See Preview.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: Control Description f(x) Python/NumPy expression — x is the independent variable array X min Start of the X range X max End of the X range N points Number of evenly spaced points in the range X col name Column name for the X dataset Y col name Column name for the generated Y dataset

docs.title: Expression syntax
docs.text:
The expression field accepts any valid NumPy expression. The variable x is a NumPy array. Common functions available without a prefix:

sin(x)          cos(x)          tan(x)
exp(x)          log(x)          log10(x)
sqrt(x)         abs(x)          sign(x)
pi              e

Examples:

sin(x) * exp(-0.1 * x)
x**2 - 3*x + 2
log(x + 1) / (1 + cos(x))

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Enter an expression in the f(x) field.
  2. Set the X range and number of points.
  3. Name the X and Y columns.
  4. Click Generate — the columns appear in the Datasets list and can be assigned to series in Plots → Plot.

Clicking Generate again with the same column names does not replace the previous data: the new columns get a numeric suffix (x_1, y_1, …).

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
Below the expression, a small plot shows what Generate would create, without creating anything. It uses the same calculation as the button, so what you see is what you get.

  • Preview draws it once. Live (on by default) redraws shortly after any change: expression, range, number of points, spacing or names.
  • With the column input, the source column is drawn in grey and the result over it.
  • logspace and geomspace get a logarithmic x axis; log y is optional.
  • With random or uniform spacing the preview keeps the same random draw until you click Generate, and the columns created are exactly the ones shown. The next preview is a new draw.
  • Problems (syntax errors, unknown names, an empty range) are written in the plot area instead of showing a dialog.
  • A line under the plot gives the number of points and the names of the columns that would be created. Above 50,000 points Live pauses; use Preview.

docs.title: z = f(x, y) and (u, v) = f(x, y)
docs.text:
The other two pages of the generator evaluate an expression of two variables, x and y, for the z column of a surface, or two expressions, u and v, for the components of a vector field.

The z=f(x,y) page:

  1. z = f(x, y) generator — Meshgrid combines every x with every y.
  2. x series — A generated range (with its spacing) or an existing column, and the name of the variable.
  3. y series — The same for y.
  4. z series — The expression, written with the two variables, and the name of the z column.
  5. Preview — The field as contours, or as points when Meshgrid is off.

The (u,v)=f(x,y) page has the same x and y series, and an expression for each component:

  1. (u, v) = f(x, y) generator — Meshgrid combines every x with every y.
  2. x series — A generated range or an existing column.
  3. y series — The same for y.
  4. u series — The expression and the name of the horizontal component.
  5. v series — The expression and the name of the vertical component.

  6. Preview — The vector field as arrows.

  7. Each axis is its own choice: a generated range (with its spacing) or an existing column, used as it is.

  8. Meshgrid combines every x with every y (nx × ny points), which is what heatmaps, contours, surfaces and vector fields need. Without it, x and y are paired point by point.
  9. The columns created are x and y (only when generated, or with a meshgrid) and z, or u and v. Names already in use get a numeric suffix.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
Both pages have the same Preview and Live as the function generator, and the plot shows what the button would create without creating anything:

  • z: a meshgrid as filled contours with their lines, otherwise coloured points (x and y paired one by one). The line under the plot gives the range of z.
  • (u, v): arrows coloured by their length, at most 20 per side on a grid. The line gives the range of the length.
  • Random and uniform spacing keep their draw until you click the button, and x and y are different draws.

docs.title: Data Table
docs.text:
The data table provides a manual spreadsheet-style entry grid for small datasets.

The Table page: set the number of columns (Cols) and rows (Rows) and click New. Below the table, +R, −R, +C and −C add and remove rows and columns, the bin button clears it, the clipboard button pastes CSV text, Load opens a CSV or Excel file into the table and CSV copies the table to the clipboard as CSV. The sections below explain each one.

docs.title: Creating a table
docs.text:
1. Set the Cols and Rows spinboxes.
  2. Click New to create a blank table.
  3. Click any cell and type to enter values.
  4. Double-click a column header to rename it.

docs.title: Editing
docs.text: Button Action ＋R Add a row at the bottom －R Delete selected rows (or the last row if none selected) ＋C Add a column on the right －C Delete the rightmost column 🗑 Clear all cell contents

docs.title: Importing data
docs.text:
• 📋 (Paste) — paste tab- or comma-separated text from the clipboard directly into the table.
  • 📥 Load — open a CSV or Excel file; its contents fill the table.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text: • 📤 CSV — copies the entire table as CSV text to the clipboard, ready to paste into another application.

docs.title: Using the table data
docs.text:
Click Apply to chart (or the equivalent generate button depending on the UI layout) to load the table's columns into the Datasets list. They become available in the series table X/Y dropdowns just like data loaded from a file.

Column names are taken from the table headers. Values that cannot be parsed as numbers are treated as categorical strings.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or later
  • macOS 11+, Windows 10+, or Linux (X11/Wayland)

docs.title: Pre-built binary (recommended — no Python required)
docs.text:
Download the latest release for your platform from GitHub:

macOS DMG / Windows ZIP → GitHub Releases

  • macOS — open the .dmg, drag plotviz.app to Applications.
  • Windows — extract the .zip and run plotviz.exe.

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text: pip install plotviz

docs.title: From source (recommended for development)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/pcachim/plotviz.git
cd plotviz
uv sync          # installs all dependencies into .venv
uv run plotviz   # launches the app

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
plotviz installs these packages automatically:

Package Version Purpose PyQt6 ≥ 6.5 UI framework matplotlib ≥ 3.7 Chart rendering seaborn ≥ 0.13 Statistical charts numpy ≥ 1.24 Numerical arrays pandas ≥ 2.0 Data loading scipy ≥ 1.10 Curve fitting and statistics statsmodels ≥ 0.14 Regression and LOWESS openpyxl ≥ 3.1 Excel file support platformdirs ≥ 3.0 Settings directory

docs.title: Launching
docs.text:
# if installed via pip
plotviz

# from source with uv
uv run plotviz

# open a file directly
plotviz mydata.pviz

You can also double-click a .pviz, .pvizt, .pvizc or .pvizp file in Finder (macOS) or Explorer (Windows) once the app is installed.

docs.title: Interface overview
docs.text:
The window has five zones:

  1. Menu bar — File (open, save, export), Edit (undo, redo, copy the chart as an image), View, Tools and Help. On macOS, About and Preferences are under the plotviz menu.
  2. Top bar — New, Open, Save, Export, and Undo / Redo for the last changes.
  3. Panel tabs — Data, Layout & Style and Plots: all the settings of the chart. Each has its own pages, described in the User Guide.
  4. Canvas toolbar — The matplotlib tools for the preview: home, back and forward, pan, zoom and the others.
  5. Chart preview — The chart as it will be exported. It redraws as you change settings. The dashed rectangle is the edge of the page (the figure size set in Layout & Style).

The plotviz window has two main areas:

Left panel — tabs

Tab Purpose Data Loaded datasets, and the Generate, Statistics and Transform pages Layout & Style Whole-figure settings: size, margins, title, subplot grid, colour scheme, palette Plots Per-subplot settings, with a Editing selector at the top when there are several subplots

The Plots tab has five pages: Plot (chart type, series table, options), Curves (per-curve line style, marker, colour, curve fitting), Axes (subplot title, axis labels, limits, scales, ticks, secondary Y axis, Z axis and 3D viewpoint), Canvas & Grid (plot-area colour, borders, major and minor grid) and Legend & Notes (legend, text/arrow/image annotations). Opening, saving and exporting are in the File menu.

Right panel — canvas

The live chart preview updates as you change settings. Use the matplotlib toolbar at the top of the canvas to pan, zoom, and reset the view.

docs.title: 1. Load data
docs.text: Click the Data tab → Browse Files and open a CSV, Excel, JSON or TXT file. plotviz reads all numeric and categorical columns and lists them in the dataset panel.

docs.title: 2. Assign columns to series
docs.text: In Plots → Plot, in the series table, use the X and Y dropdowns to pick which columns to plot. The Label column sets the legend entry. Add more rows with the + Add series button.

docs.title: 3. Choose a chart type
docs.text: In Plots → Plot, select a chart type from the dropdown — Line, Scatter, Bar, and so on. The canvas updates instantly.

docs.title: 4. Style the chart
docs.text:
• Layout & Style tab: set background color, colour scheme, figure size.
  • Plots → Curves: change line color, width, marker style.
  • Plots → Axes: set axis labels, limits, scale, grid and canvas colours.
  • Plots → Legend & Notes: add a legend or text annotations. The subplot title is in Plots → Axes.

docs.title: 5. Export
docs.text:
Click ⬆ Export in the top bar (or File → Export Image…, Ctrl+E), pick a format (PNG, SVG, PDF, JPEG) and a DPI, then Save… to write a file or Copy to clipboard to paste the image into another app (raster formats only). The DPI and figure dimensions set in the Layout & Style tab are used for the exported file.

With more than one subplot, tick Also save each subplot as its own file to get, besides the whole figure, one file per subplot (name_1, name_2, …). Each keeps its own proportions; raster files are scaled so the longer side matches the longer side of the figure, and vector files (SVG, PDF, EPS) keep the subplot's natural size. A subplot file includes its axis labels, twin axis, legend and colorbar, but not the figure title or a figure-wide legend. Existing files with those names are replaced after you confirm.

docs.title: 6. Save your work
docs.text: Click Save Chart (.pviz) to save a .pviz project file. Reopening it restores your data, series assignments, and all style settings.

docs.title: Settings and preferences
docs.text:
plotviz stores user preferences in a JSON file:

Platform Location macOS ~/Library/Application Support/plotviz/settings.json Linux ~/.config/plotviz/settings.json Windows %APPDATA%\plotviz\settings.json

Stored preferences include the last-used directory, theme (System/Light/Dark), recent files list (up to 12), recent colors; your colour schemes and palettes are files in the schemes and palettes folders beside it, and window geometry.

docs.title: Appearance (light and dark)
docs.text:
The Colour scheme dropdown in the Preferences window (plotviz → Preferences… on macOS, Edit → Settings… on Windows and Linux) controls the application's light and dark mode:

  • System — follows the OS theme (default).
  • Light — forces the light theme.
  • Dark — forces the dark theme.

This changes the application only, not the chart colours, which are set with Color Schemes and the Layout & Style tab.

To reset all settings to defaults, delete the settings.json file and restart the app.

docs.title: Layout & Style
docs.text:
The Layout & Style tab controls the figure as a whole: size, margins, title, subplot layout, colour scheme and palette. The plot area, borders and grid of each subplot are on the Plots → Canvas & Grid page.

From top to bottom:

  1. Figure — The page: a preset or your own width and height, in the unit you choose.
  2. Margins — The distance from the page edge to the plot area, in the same unit. Show margin mask shades the margins on the preview.
  3. Subplots — Configure Subplot Layout… opens the grid and mosaic dialog; H spacing and W spacing set the gaps between panels.
  4. Title — Show or hide the chart title, its text, font, size and colour.
  5. Position & rotation — Where the title sits on the page (X, Y), its rotation and its alignment.
  6. Colors — The colour settings of the whole figure: the two sections below.
  7. Color schemes — The scheme (backgrounds, text, grid, borders) and, with several subplots, whether it applies to all of them or to one. Edit, Load and Save manage your own.
  8. Colour palette — The colours given to the curves in order. Edit, Load and Save manage your own palettes; Re-apply palette gives the curves the palette colours again.

docs.title: Figure size
docs.text:
Control Description Preset Quick size: A4 landscape, Letter, 20×15 cm (default), 16×9 widescreen, square Unit cm, inches, or px Width / Height Exact dimensions in the chosen unit

The size set here is used for both the live preview and the exported file.

docs.title: Margins
docs.text: Four boxes — Left, Right, Bottom, Top — give the distance from the page edge to the plot area, in the unit chosen above. The defaults leave room for axis labels and the title. Show margin mask shades the margins on the preview so you can see what they control.

docs.title: DPI
docs.text: The resolution of exported PNG and JPEG files is chosen in the Export dialog. SVG and PDF are vector formats and ignore it.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Subplots — the grid and mosaic dialog behind Configure Subplot Layout….
  • Color Schemes and Color Palettes — the Colors section.
  • Axes — the title of each subplot and the axis labels.
  • Canvas & Grid — the plot area, borders and grid of each subplot.

docs.title: Legend and Notes
docs.text:
The Legend & Notes tab manages what is drawn on and around the data: the legend, and free-form text, arrow and image annotations placed directly on the chart. (The title of each subplot is in the Axes tab.)

When the chart has more than one subplot, the Subplot selector at the top of the tab switches context. All controls — legend, annotation visibility — apply to the currently selected subplot.

The page, from top to bottom:

  1. Legend — Show it, place it (automatically or at coordinates), its font size, columns, frame and colours.
  2. Place annotation — Choose what a click on the chart does: nothing (Normal / Drag), or add a Text, an Arrow or an Image.
  3. Style for new annotations — Font, size and colours of what you add next. Below it you can also type the position and click Place, and use Undo last or Clear all.
  4. Annotations — double-click to edit — The list of the annotations of this subplot. Double-click one to edit it, or use Edit selected and Delete selected.

docs.title: Visibility and position
docs.text:
Control Description Show legend Checkbox — toggle legend on/off for this subplot Position Placement preset: best, upper right, upper left, upper center, lower right, lower left, lower center, center right, center left, center, manual X / Y Fine position adjustment as a figure fraction (0.0–1.5). Active for all positions except best.

When Position is set to anything other than best, the X and Y spinboxes act as bbox_to_anchor coordinates — the selected corner of the legend box is pinned to that point. For example, "upper right" at X=0.98, Y=0.98 places the top-right corner of the legend near the top-right of the axes.

When Position is best, matplotlib automatically finds the location with the least overlap with the data.

docs.title: Style
docs.text: Control Description Font sz Font size for legend entries (pt) Cols Number of columns in the legend (1–8) Frame Checkbox — show the legend box border Text color Color of legend label text BG color Background fill color of the legend box α Background opacity (0.0–1.0) Edge color Border color of the legend box

docs.title: Annotation visibility
docs.text: The Show annotations on this subplot checkbox hides or shows all text, arrow, and image annotations on the selected subplot without deleting them.

docs.title: Placing annotations
docs.text:
Four mode buttons select the current annotation tool:

Button Mode 🖱 Normal/Drag Selection and drag mode — click an annotation to select it, drag to move 📝 Text Click anywhere on the chart to place a text label ➡ Arrow Click the start point, then click the end point to draw an arrow 🖼 Image Opens a file picker; click on the chart to place the image

docs.title: Text annotations
docs.text: After clicking in text mode, a dialog opens to enter the label text. The annotation is placed at the clicked coordinates.

docs.title: Arrow annotations
docs.text: Click once to set the arrow tail (start), then click again to set the arrowhead (end). A text label can be attached to the arrow tail.

docs.title: Image annotations
docs.text: Select an image file (PNG, JPEG, etc.), then click on the chart to place it. Use the Img zoom spinbox to set the initial display size as a fraction of the figure.

docs.title: Manual coordinate placement
docs.text: Enter exact data-coordinate values in the X and Y fields and click 📍 Place to position the next text annotation precisely.

docs.title: Annotation style
docs.text:
Controls in the Style for new annotations section set the default appearance applied to annotations placed after the change. They do not retroactively change existing annotations.

Control Description Font / Sz Font family and size Font color Text color BG / α Background fill color and opacity Border Box border color

docs.title: Managing annotations
docs.text:
The Annotations list at the bottom of the tab shows all annotations on the current subplot. Each entry shows the type icon and either the label text or coordinates.

Double-click any entry to open an edit dialog where you can change the text, position, font, colors, and border of that annotation.

The ✏️ Edit selected and 🗑 Delete selected buttons provide the same actions via keyboard/click.

↩ Undo last removes the most recently placed annotation.

🗑 Clear all removes every annotation from the current subplot.

docs.title: Color Palettes
docs.text: A color palette is an ordered list of 16 colors used as the default cycle for series in a chart. When a new series is added, the next color in the active palette is assigned automatically.

docs.title: Selecting a palette
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, choose a palette from the Color palette dropdown. The chart updates immediately, reassigning colors to all series that do not have a locked color.

docs.title: Built-in palettes
docs.text:
plotviz ships with 11 palettes:

Name Character Matplotlib The standard matplotlib default color cycle — blue, orange, green, red, purple, brown, pink, grey, yellow-green, cyan Pastel Soft, desaturated tones — baby blue, peach, mint, rose, periwinkle Bold High-contrast vivid colors — red, green, blue, orange, purple, cyan, magenta, lime Earth Warm browns, greens and greys — saddle brown, olive, khaki, forest green Ocean Deep cool blues through warm orange — navy, indigo, purple, magenta, coral, amber Warm Reds, oranges and yellows — crimson, tangerine, gold, coral, amber Cool Blues, greens and purples — steel blue, teal, sage, lavender, sky Colorblind Optimized for the most common forms of color vision deficiency (deuteranopia, protanopia) Nature Muted greens, blues and earthy tones — teal, burnt orange, coral, dark blue Publication Black + strong, distinct hues suitable for print — black, red, blue, green, purple, orange Grayscale Black through white in even steps — for monochrome print or accessibility

docs.title: Custom palettes
docs.text: Palettes work like colour schemes: the built-in ones are read-only, and your own are files. Every .pvizp in the palettes folder is loaded when plotviz starts. Its location is shown in Preferences (Colour palettes), next to a button that opens it; on macOS it is ~/Library/Application Support/plotviz/palettes/.

docs.title: Creating or editing a palette
docs.text:
1. In the Layout & Style tab, click Edit palette…. It opens with the colours of the active palette; Load from starts from another one.
  2. Give it a name and click each of the 16 swatches to set the colours.
  3. Click Save & apply. The palette becomes the active one.

Opening the editor on one of your own palettes edits it in place. Built-in names cannot be replaced.

A * after a palette's name in the dropdown means it is not in the palettes folder, so it will not be there next time. A new palette starts that way; saving it into the folder removes the *.

docs.title: Sharing and keeping palettes
docs.text:
Save: click Save under Colour palette. The dialog opens in the palettes folder; you can save anywhere else too, but a file outside the folder keeps its * and is not loaded at start-up. Built-in palettes cannot be saved, since they are always there. To delete a palette, delete its file.

Load: click Load and choose a single .pvizp file (for instance one from outside the folder). With one palette in the file you are asked whether to apply it.

A chart file (.pviz) carries its active palette when it is one of yours, so the chart opens with the same colours.

docs.title: Re-applying the palette
docs.text:
Series whose colour you set by hand keep it when you change palette or scheme. ↺ Re-apply palette (under the Edit / Load / Save buttons) gives every series its palette colour again, those included.

See File Formats for the .pvizp format specification.

docs.title: Color locking
docs.text:
By default, switching palettes reassigns all series colors to match the new palette. To preserve a specific series' color across palette switches, tick Lock color in the Series tab for that series.

Locked colors are shown with a lock icon in the series color swatch. They are never modified by palette changes, but can still be changed manually by clicking the swatch.

docs.title: Recent colors in the color picker
docs.text: The color picker dialog shows a Recent colors row above the Custom colors section. It stores the last 8 colors you selected (across all color pickers in the app) and persists them between sessions. Click any recent swatch to instantly reuse that color.

docs.title: Plot: Series and Chart Types
docs.text: The Plots → Plot page decides what is drawn: which columns, as which chart type, in which subplot. Everything else about how it looks is on the other pages of the Plots tab.

docs.title: The series table
docs.text:
The series table is on the Plots → Plot page:

  1. Plot mode — Which group of chart types the subplot uses: Standard, Histogram, Statistical, Heatmap & Contour, Polar & Radar, Pie or Quiver.
  2. Series — One row per plotted series: the X and Y columns, the legend Label, the chart Type, the number of the subplot it belongs to (Plot) and whether it uses the secondary axis (Y2). Add series and Remove selected change the rows. Below the table, the options of the selected series appear.
Column Purpose X Column used as the horizontal axis values Y Column used as the vertical axis values Label Text shown in the chart legend Type Chart type for this series (Line, Scatter, Bar, …) Plot Which subplot panel this series appears in (1-based) Y2 Checkbox — plots this series on the secondary Y axis

docs.title: Adding and removing series
docs.text:
• + Add series — appends a new row with empty column selections.
  • − Remove selected — removes the selected rows.

docs.title: Mixing chart types
docs.text:
Each row in the series table has its own Type dropdown, so you can mix chart types within the same panel — for example, a Line series and a Scatter series sharing the same axes.

Types that take over the whole chart (Histogram, Pie, Heatmap, etc.) cannot be mixed with other types in the same subplot.

docs.title: Secondary Y axis (Y2)
docs.text: Tick the Y2 checkbox on any series row to plot it against a second Y axis on the right side of the chart. The Y2 axis label is set in the Axes tab.

docs.title: Z column and error column
docs.text:
Below the series table are two extra dropdowns:

  • Z — used by Heatmap, Hist2D, Hexbin, Contour, and Bubble charts as the third data dimension.
  • Error — used by the Errorbar chart as the error/uncertainty values.

docs.title: Chart type selection
docs.text:
The Plot mode dropdown at the top of Plots → Plot chooses a group of chart types for the subplot: Standard, Histogram, Statistical, Heatmap & Contour, Polar & Radar, Pie or Quiver. The Type cell of each series offers the types of that group.

In Standard the type belongs to each series, so they can be mixed; the other groups draw the whole panel as one chart.

See Chart Types for a full description of every chart type and its options.

docs.title: Python Export Bundle
docs.text: The Python Export Bundle feature converts any plotviz chart into a self-contained Python project — a ZIP archive (.pvizx) that includes a standalone matplotlib script and the chart's data as CSV files. The exported script has no dependency on plotviz and can be run, shared, and modified in any Python environment.

docs.title: Save to file
docs.text:
Go to File → Export Python Bundle (.pvizx)… (or use the corresponding menu shortcut).

A save dialog appears with a suggested filename based on the current chart title. Choose a location and click Save.

After the export completes, a confirmation message shows the full file path. The bundle can be extracted and run immediately:

unzip mychart.pvizx -d mychart
cd mychart
python plot.py

docs.title: Send directly to Code Runner
docs.text: Use Tools → Code Runner from chart (or the ▶ Open in Code Runner button in the Seaborn Explorer) to skip the save dialog entirely. plotviz writes the bundle to a temporary location and opens it in the Python Code Runner so you can inspect and edit the generated script right away.

docs.title: Bundle contents
docs.text:
A .pvizx file is a standard ZIP archive with the following structure:

mychart.pvizx
├── plot.py          # Standalone matplotlib script
├── README.md        # Quick-start instructions
├── pyproject.toml   # Optional: dependency declaration
└── data/
    ├── data.csv     # All columns (when they share the same length)
    │   — or —
    ├── column1.csv  # One CSV per column (when lengths differ)
    └── column2.csv

docs.title: plot.py
docs.text:
The main script is completely standalone — it imports only standard scientific Python packages and reads its data from the data/ folder relative to its own location. It faithfully reproduces:

  • All chart types and subplot layouts
  • Axis labels, limits, scales, and tick formatting
  • Series colors, line widths, markers, and fill styles
  • Curve fits with optional confidence and prediction bands
  • Title, legend, grid, and figure size

docs.title: data/
docs.text: Date columns are written to the CSV as ISO 8601 text (2024-03-01, 2024-03-01T12:30:00), and the script converts them back with pd.to_datetime, so the exported chart has a date axis too. Only the columns actually assigned to series in the chart are exported. If all exported columns share the same row count, they are written to a single data/data.csv. If they differ in length, each column gets its own CSV file (e.g. data/pressure.csv) to avoid NaN padding.

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text: A minimal pyproject.toml listing the required packages (matplotlib, numpy, pandas, scipy) for use with tools like uv or pip.

docs.title: Running the exported script
docs.text:
Requirements (installed automatically if using pyproject.toml):

pip install matplotlib numpy pandas scipy

Then run:

python plot.py

The chart is displayed in a matplotlib window. To save it instead, call plt.savefig('output.png', dpi=300) at the end of the script.

docs.title: Opening a .pvizx bundle
docs.text:
You can re-open any .pvizx file in the Python Code Runner to edit the generated script interactively:

  1. Open the Code Runner: Tools → Python Code Runner…
  2. Click 📦 Load .pvizx… and select the bundle.
  3. plotviz extracts the archive, loads plot.py into the editor, and runs it automatically.

You can also double-click a .pvizx file in Finder (macOS) or Explorer (Windows) to open it directly in the Code Runner, if plotviz is set as the default application for that file type.

docs.title: Supported chart types
docs.text:
All 22 plotviz chart types are supported in the Python export, including:

Line, Scatter, Step, Area, Bar, Stem, Error Bar, Histogram, Boxplot, Violin, Pie, Polar, Radar, Heatmap, Contour, Tricontour, 3D Surface, ECDF, 2D Histogram, Hexbin, Quiver, Barbs, Streamplot

Seaborn charts created in the Seaborn Explorer can be exported via the 🐍 Generate Python Code or ▶ Open in Code Runner buttons in that dialog.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The exported script uses absolute file paths resolved relative to plot.py, so keep plot.py and the data/ folder together.
  • plotviz-specific features like drag-and-drop annotations and the manual data table are reproduced in the script as static data.
  • The .pvizx extension is not a standard zip alias on all platforms — use an explicit unzip command or a ZIP tool if double-clicking does not extract it outside of plotviz.

docs.title: Seaborn Explorer
docs.text:
The Seaborn Explorer is a dedicated dialog for creating statistical charts powered by seaborn. It runs on its own canvas, fully isolated from the main plotviz chart, so figure-level seaborn plots (Pairplot, Joint, Heatmap, Catplot) never interfere with the main chart's style pipeline.

Open it from the menu bar: Tools → Seaborn Explorer…

Requirements

Seaborn must be installed: pip install seaborn. Some regression options (Robust fit, LOWESS) additionally require pip install statsmodels.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
The window has two panels:

Panel Contents Left — controls Chart type, color theme, column selectors, and chart-specific options Right — preview Live seaborn canvas with navigation toolbar and export controls

Changes to the controls do not redraw automatically — click Redraw to apply them.

docs.title: Chart types
docs.text: Type Description KDE Kernel Density Estimate — smoothed distribution curve Regression Scatter plot with OLS, polynomial, or LOWESS regression line Strip Categorical scatter plot with jitter Swarm Categorical beeswarm plot (non-overlapping points) Heatmap Correlation matrix heatmap Pairplot All-vs-all scatter grid (uses column picker) Joint Bivariate joint distribution with marginals Catplot Figure-level categorical chart (box, violin, bar, strip, and more)

docs.title: Data columns
docs.text:
For chart types that use X/Y axes (KDE, Regression, Strip, Swarm, Joint, Catplot), select columns from the dropdowns:

Dropdown Accepts X column Any loaded column (numeric or categorical) Y column Numeric columns only Hue (category) Categorical columns — splits data into color groups Size (category) Categorical columns — varies marker size by group Style (category) Categorical columns — varies marker shape/line style by group

For Heatmap and Pairplot, a multi-select column list replaces the X/Y dropdowns. Use All / None buttons to quickly select or deselect all numeric columns.

docs.title: Color theme
docs.text:
The Palette dropdown controls the color scheme used for all chart types. The first option, plotviz, applies your current plotviz color palette. All other options are standard seaborn/matplotlib named palettes:

deep, muted, pastel, bright, dark, colorblind, tab10, Set1, Set2, Set3, Paired, husl, hls, rocket, mako, flare, crest, viridis, plasma, magma, inferno

Note

Robust fit and LOWESS are mutually exclusive with each other and with polynomial order > 1.
