docs.title: Canvas controls
docs.text: The matplotlib navigation toolbar above the preview canvas provides pan, zoom, and reset controls. See Keyboard Shortcuts for details.

docs.title: Bottom bar
docs.text: Button Description Redraw Re-render the chart with the current control values DPI spinner Export resolution (72–600 DPI) Export… Save the chart as PNG, SVG, PDF, or JPEG 🐍 Generate Python Code Show a standalone Python script that reproduces the current chart ▶ Open in Code Runner Export the chart as a .pvizx bundle and open it in the Python Code Runner Close Close the Seaborn Explorer

docs.title: Generating Python code
docs.text:
Click 🐍 Generate Python Code to view a standalone Python script that reproduces the current seaborn chart without any dependency on plotviz. You can copy and paste this script into any Python environment.

Click ▶ Open in Code Runner to send the chart directly to the Python Code Runner, where you can edit and re-run the generated code interactively.

docs.title: Global shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl + N New chart Ctrl + O Open chart Ctrl + S Save chart (rewrites the open file; asks where the first time) Ctrl + Shift + S Save chart as… Ctrl + L Load data Ctrl + E Export image Ctrl + Shift + E Export Python bundle Ctrl + Z Undo Ctrl + Y or Ctrl + Shift + Z Redo Ctrl + Shift + C Copy the chart as an image (Ctrl + C keeps copying text in fields and tables) Ctrl + , (macOS) / Ctrl + Alt + S Preferences / Settings Ctrl + Shift + B Seaborn Explorer Ctrl + Shift + P Python Code Runner Ctrl + Shift + R Code Runner from the current chart F1 Documentation (opens in its own window; Help → Documentation Online opens the website)

docs.title: Tab navigation (View menu)
docs.text:
The View menu lists the three tabs as checkable items; the active one is ticked.

Menu item Tab View → Data Datasets, Generate, Statistics and Transform pages View → Layout & Style Figure size, margins, title, subplot grid, colour scheme, palette View → Plots Per-subplot settings: Plot, Curves, Axes, Canvas & Grid, Legend & Notes

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Edit → Undo and Redo (and the two buttons in the top bar) step through up to 50 changes. Hover over a button to see what it will undo or redo ("Undo: Apply fit"), and the status bar says what was undone.

A step is recorded about half a second after the last change, so a burst of edits (typing, dragging a spin box) is one step. Everything that makes up the chart is in it:

  • every setting, per subplot, including the style of each curve;
  • the datasets (loading, removing, Generate, Transform, the data table);
  • the series table and the fits (with their bands, and whether each is shown);
  • the annotations (adding, moving, editing, deleting).

After an undo you stay on the same subplot and curve, and the lists keep their selection. Undo does not cover zooming or panning with the toolbar, the open/save state of the file, or the palettes you saved to disk.

The history starts again when you open a file or start a new chart. The datasets in the history are not copied: a step only holds the arrays that changed, so a long history does not multiply the memory used by large data.

docs.title: Canvas (matplotlib toolbar)
docs.text:
The toolbar above the chart canvas provides standard matplotlib navigation:

Button Action 🏠 Home Reset to the original view ◀ Back Go to the previous view ▶ Forward Go to the next view ✛ Pan Click and drag to pan; right-drag to zoom 🔍 Zoom Draw a rectangle to zoom in ⚙ Subplots Adjust subplot spacing (matplotlib built-in) 💾 Save Save the figure via matplotlib's own dialog

docs.title: Annotation mode shortcuts
docs.text:
While in the Legend & Notes tab:

Key Action Esc Exit the current annotation placement mode and return to Normal/Drag

docs.title: Color picker
docs.text: Key Action Enter Confirm the selected color (OK) Esc Cancel and close the color picker

docs.title: Series click-to-select
docs.text: Click directly on a plotted series in the canvas to jump to the Series tab with that series pre-selected. This works for line, scatter, bar, and most other series types.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
The Data → Statistics page summarises the loaded series. To create new series from them, see Transform.

The Statistics page summarises the loaded series. It works on the series selected in the Datasets list, or on all of them when none is selected. It refreshes when you open the page; click ↻ Refresh after changing the selection or the data.

The Statistics page:

  1. Summary — A table with count, missing values, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and more, one column per series (the ones selected in the Datasets list, or all of them).
  2. Correlation — The correlation matrix of the series, with the Method (Pearson or Spearman). Refresh recalculates and Copy summary puts the table on the clipboard.

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text:
One column per series and one row per statistic:

Statistic Meaning count Valid values (NaN and infinity are not counted) missing NaN, infinity or empty values mean, std Mean and sample standard deviation (n − 1) min, 25%, median, 75%, max Range and quartiles skew, kurtosis Skewness and excess kurtosis (a normal distribution has 0 for both)

Text series only get count and missing. For date series the mean, minimum, quartiles, median and maximum are shown as dates, and the standard deviation is in days. Cells that cannot be computed (the std of one value, the skew of a constant series) are left blank.

📋 Copy summary copies the table to the clipboard, tab-separated, ready to paste into a spreadsheet.

docs.title: Correlation matrix
docs.text:
Below the summary, the correlation between every pair of numeric series, with cells shaded red for positive and blue for negative values. Choose the Method:

  • pearson — linear correlation.
  • spearman — rank correlation; detects any monotonic relationship, linear or not, and is less sensitive to outliers.

Each pair uses only the points where both series are valid. A cell is blank when the two series have different lengths, one of them is constant, or there are fewer than 3 common points.

docs.title: Subplots
docs.text: plotviz supports multi-panel layouts with up to 9 subplots per chart. Each subplot is an independent axes with its own series, title, labels, limits, legend, and annotations.

docs.title: Opening the layout dialog
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, click ⚙️ Configure Subplot Layout… to open the layout picker.

docs.title: Layout presets
docs.text: The Presets tab shows a visual gallery of 18 built-in layouts. Click a preview thumbnail to select it; the chart updates immediately.

docs.title: Regular grids
docs.text: Preset Description Single 1 × 1 (default) 1 × 2 One row, two columns 1 × 3 One row, three columns 2 × 1 Two rows, one column 2 × 2 Two rows, two columns 2 × 3 Two rows, three columns 3 × 1 Three rows, one column 3 × 2 Three rows, two columns 3 × 3 Three rows, three columns

docs.title: Mosaic presets (unequal panels)
docs.text: Preset Description 1 top / 2 down Wide panel on top, two panels below 2 top / 1 down Two panels on top, wide panel below 1 left / 2 right Tall panel on the left, two panels stacked on the right 2 left / 1 right Two panels stacked on the left, tall panel on the right 1 top / 3 down Wide panel on top, three panels in a row below 3 top / 1 down Three panels in a row on top, wide panel below 2×2 mosaic 1+1+2 Two equal panels above, one wide panel below 3 rows / 1 wide top Three rows: wide top, two-column middle, two-column bottom 3 rows / 1 wide bottom Three rows: two-column top, two-column middle, wide bottom

docs.title: Custom mosaic editor
docs.text:
The Custom mosaic tab provides a grid editor for building any layout.

  1. Set the Rows and Columns spinboxes to define the grid dimensions.
  2. Each cell in the grid shows a letter label. Click cells to assign them to the same panel (merge) or reset them to individual panels.
  3. The mosaic is described as a 2D list of letters, e.g. [['A','A'],['B','C']] for a wide top panel over two equal bottom panels.

docs.title: Live preview
docs.text: A small preview thumbnail updates as you edit the mosaic, showing the resulting panel layout.

docs.title: Shared axes
docs.text:
Two checkboxes in the layout dialog configure axis sharing:

Option Effect Share X axis All subplots in the same column share their X limits and tick marks Share Y axis All subplots in the same row share their Y limits and tick marks

Shared axes keep panels visually aligned and make comparisons easier.

docs.title: Assigning series to subplots
docs.text:
In the Data tab series table, the Plot # column sets which subplot (1-based) a series appears in. Increment the number to move a series to a different panel.

The Axes and Legend & Notes tabs both have a Subplot selector at the top that lets you configure each panel independently. All three selectors (Axes, Legend & Notes, Series) stay in sync — changing one updates the others.

docs.title: Per-subplot settings
docs.text:
Each subplot has its own independent settings for:

  • Title text, font, size, and color
  • X, Y, and Y2 axis labels
  • Axis limits (auto or manual) for X, Y, and Y2
  • Axis scale (linear, log, logit, inverted)
  • Tick configuration (size, direction, minor ticks, rotation, step, formatter)
  • Legend (show/hide, position, style)
  • Annotation visibility
  • Canvas background, borders, grid and 3D view (Canvas & Grid tab)

Changes made in the Axes and Legend & Notes tabs always apply to the subplot currently shown in the selector.

When you add subplots, the new ones start with the look of the active subplot: fonts and sizes, tick and legend style, label layout, canvas colours and grid. What depends on the data (titles and labels, limits, scale, tick step, number format, chart type) starts empty or at its default.

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
The Data → Transform page creates new series from existing ones: smoothing, decimation, calculus, scaling, cleaning, resampling and signal analysis. To summarise series instead, see Statistics.

The Transform page applies an operation (smoothing, decimation, calculus, scaling, cleaning, resampling…) to a series and stores the result as a new series. The original is never changed, so you can plot both together.

The Transform page:

  1. Series — x is the horizontal axis (optional) and y the series to transform.
  2. Operation — The operation, grouped by type, and its parameters, which change with the operation.
  3. Preview — What Apply would create, without creating anything. See Preview.
  4. Result — The name of the new series (automatic when empty) and the Apply button.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
1. x — the horizontal axis (for example the time or position series). Optional: choose (none: use index) when the series has no x column. Operations that need an x (resampling, cropping, sorting, aligning) report an error without it. Derivatives and integrals use the index as the spacing when there is no x.
  2. y — the series to transform (the values: the signal, the measurement). Swapping x and y gives odd results, because the result is calculated as a function of x: resampling y_irregular over t_irregular is a different curve from resampling t_irregular over y_irregular.
  3. Operation — pick it from the list, which is grouped by type (the group names are bold headers).
  4. Set the parameters, which change with the operation.
  5. Optionally type a Name for the result; the default is the series name plus a suffix, for example signal_MA5.
  6. Click Apply.

The status line under the button says what was created and how many points it has. New series appear at once in the Datasets list and in the series table.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
Below the parameters, a small plot shows what Apply would create, without creating anything: the original series in grey and the result on top of it. It uses the same calculation as Apply, so what you see is what you get.

  • Preview draws it once. Live (on by default) redraws shortly after any change — series, operation or parameter.
  • Peaks are drawn as markers. A spectrum is drawn alone, since its x axis is different. Date columns get a date axis. log y helps with spectra.
  • Long series are drawn with a reduced number of points (the highs and lows are kept). Above 50,000 points Live pauses; use Preview.
  • Problems (a window longer than the series, no x for a resample, ...) are written in the plot area instead of showing a dialog.
  • Under the plot, a line says how many points go in and the name of the series that would be created.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
When x is a date column, the operations that keep or select x values keep it as dates: the new x series from cropping, decimating, resampling, aligning, removing NaN or finding peaks is a date series, and plots with a date axis. Notes:

  • Crop x range: type the limits as dates, for example 2024-03-01 or 1 Mar 2024 12:00. Leave a box empty for no limit.
  • Resample (uniform x), derivatives, integrals and filters work in days: the derivative is per day, and the Butterworth cutoff is in cycles per day.
  • FFT amplitude spectrum: the frequencies are in cycles per day, and are not dates.
  • Moving average, median and the other window operations count points, not time, so they assume regular sampling; use Resample (uniform x) first if the dates are irregular.

Results are calculated once

A transformed series is a copy. If you later change or reload the original data, the transformed series is not recalculated — apply the operation again.

docs.title: When x changes
docs.text:
Some operations change the number or position of the points (decimating, cropping, resampling, removing NaN, FFT, peaks…). When that happens a new x series is created next to the new y, named after the x series and the suffix, for example t_every3 and y_every3. Plot the pair together.

  • FFT and Find peaks create their own x even if you chose none: frequencies for the FFT, and the x of each peak (the point index when there is no x series).
  • Align to another x reuses the x of the series you chose instead of creating a duplicate; the status line tells you which series to use as x.

docs.title: Signal analysis
docs.text:
Operation Parameters Notes FFT amplitude spectrum Remove mean Single-sided amplitude. x gives the sampling interval, so it should be evenly spaced; y must have no NaN. Output: frequency and amplitude Find peaks Min height (× noise), min height, min prominence, min distance Local maxima. Output: only the peak points. Min height (× noise) sets the threshold at the median plus k times the noise of the series (estimated robustly, so a few peaks do not inflate it; remove any drift first). With Min height as well, the higher limit applies. Prominence is measured against the valleys around a peak, so with noise it needs about 8 times the noise level; a height threshold of about 5 times is simpler. An error is shown if there are no peaks

Recipes

  • Remove spikes, then smooth: Outlier filter (Hampel), then Savitzky-Golay on the result.
  • Find the dominant frequency: Remove trend, then FFT amplitude spectrum, and plot the spectrum.
  • Uneven sampling: Resample (uniform x) before a Butterworth filter or an FFT.
  • Pulse in a stable signal with noise: Subtract baseline (median of range, over a stretch without the pulse), then Savitzky-Golay with a window no longer than the pulse (in points), then Find peaks with Min height (× noise) of 5 or 6 and a Min distance of the pulse width. Do not use the moving median or the outlier filter: they treat the pulse as noise and remove it. For a negative pulse, Scale and shift with a = −1 first.
  • Compare two series with different x: Align to another x puts one on the x of the other.
